summary: Analytical aptitude checks whether you can follow stated rules exactly. Deduction covers syllogisms tested by Venn diagrams, conditional statements and their contrapositives, arrangement and truth-teller puzzles, blood relations and direction sense. Induction covers number and letter series, coding, odd one out and matrix patterns. Analogies ask for the same relation in a new pair, and numerical relations add inequality chains, ranks, data sufficiency and number properties such as divisibility and unit digits. Draw every case on paper and accept only what holds in all of them.
highYield: Syllogisms with two or three statements: which conclusions follow, including the either-or case. Usually a 1-mark MCQ.
Valid deduction from an if-then or only-if statement: the contrapositive is the only equivalent form.
Seating or ordering puzzles with five to eight people and adjacency clues, asked as 2-mark MCQs.
Next term of a number series built from differences, powers or two interleaved sequences, often as a NAT.
Truth-teller puzzles with a fixed count of true statements, and inequality chains that must or need not hold.

topics.title: Categorical propositions: All, No, Some, Some-not
points: Four standard forms: A "All S are P" (S lies wholly inside P), E "No S is P" (disjoint circles), I "Some S are P" (the circles share at least one member) and O "Some S are not P" (at least one S lies outside P).
"Some" means at least one and possibly all. "Some S are P" is still true when every S is P, so it never implies "Some S are not P".
"All S are P" does not give "All P are S": P may be strictly bigger. It does give "Some P are S" when S is non-empty, which aptitude questions assume.
Accept every premise as literally true, however absurd ("All dogs are clouds"). Real-world knowledge is irrelevant; only the stated relations count.
A and O contradict each other, as do E and I: exactly one of each pair is true. A and E can both be false; I and O can both be true.

lesson.why: Syllogism and consistency questions all rest on four sentence shapes, and mixing up what "some" and "all" allow is a way to lose these marks.
lesson.intro: A categorical proposition links two groups. Call them S (the subject group) and P (the predicate group). There are four shapes: "All S are P", "No S is P", "Some S are P" and "Some S are not P". Each says something exact about how the two groups overlap, and it is read literally, whatever you know about the real world.

definitions.meaning: A statement about every member of S: "All S are P" or "No S is P".
A statement about at least one member of S: "Some S are P" or "Some S are not P".
Two statements of which exactly one is true: All and Some-not, or No and Some.

principle.text: Write the four forms as A (All), E (No), I (Some) and O (Some-not). A and O are contradictories, and so are E and I. "Some" means at least one, so it allows all. Assume S has at least one member when you need A and E to exclude each other.

lesson.limits: A and O are always contradictories, and so are E and I, whether or not S has members. Non-emptiness matters elsewhere: only if S has a member are "All S are P" and "No S is P" unable to be true together, and only then does "All" imply "Some". A and E are not contradictories: both can be false, for example when some S are in P and some are not. Real-world truth never matters; accept each premise as stated.

example.problem: "All metals are conductors" is false. What can you say about "Some metals are not conductors" and "No metal is a conductor"?
steps: "All metals are conductors" is the A form, and its contradictory is the O form, "Some metals are not conductors".
Since the A form is false, the O form must be true.
"No metal is a conductor" is the E form. With the A form false, some metals may still be conductors or none may be, so the E form can be true or false.
example.result: "Some metals are not conductors" is true; "No metal is a conductor" is undetermined.

misconceptions: "Some S are P" does not mean that some S are not P. If every S is P, then "Some S are P" is still true and "Some S are not P" is false.
The opposite of "All S are P" is not "No S is P". It is "Some S are not P", because one exception is enough to break "All".

recall.q: What is the contradictory of "All S are P"?
recall.a: "Some S are not P". Exactly one of the two is true.

recall.q: Can "All S are P" and "No S is P" both be false?
recall.a: Yes, when some S are in P and some are not. They cannot both be true if S has a member.

practice.stem: The statement "No coder is tired" is false. Which statement must then be true?
practice.explanation: "No coder is tired" is the E form, and its contradictory is the I form, "Some coders are tired". The first option tempts because it is a stronger version of the same idea, but "Some" allows a coder who is not tired, so "All" is not forced. The third option is not forced either, since every coder could be tired.

lesson.summary: The four forms are All, No, Some and Some-not. All and Some-not contradict each other, as do No and Some, and "Some" always allows "All".

topics.title: Venn-diagram validity test for syllogisms
points: A conclusion follows only if it holds in every diagram consistent with the premises. One consistent diagram where it fails is enough to reject it.
Draw the most restrictive picture the premises force, then try to break each conclusion by stretching circles: let "Some" become "All", or let an unconstrained circle sit outside or inside another.
Chains that always work: All A–B and All B–C give All A–C; All A–B and No B–C give No A–C; Some A–B and All B–C give Some A–C; Some A–B and No B–C give Some A are not C.
Two "Some" premises (Some A are B, Some B are C) give no definite link between A and C: the shared B members may or may not be the same.
Either-or (complementary pair): when neither "Some A are C" nor "No A is C" follows on its own, the answer is "Either I or II follows", because the two are contradictories and one must hold.
Without a definite relation, "possibility" conclusions ("All A being C is a possibility") follow when at least one consistent diagram makes them true.

lesson.why: Syllogism questions ask which conclusions follow from two premises, and a Venn test settles each one without relying on instinct about the words.
lesson.intro: A conclusion follows only if it is true in every picture that fits the premises. So draw the premises as overlapping circles, then ask whether the conclusion can fail in any allowed picture. If one allowed picture breaks it, the conclusion does not follow, however natural it sounds. Draw "All X are Y" as circle X inside circle Y, "No X is Y" as two separate circles, and "Some X are Y" as overlapping circles with a marked member in the overlap.

definitions.meaning: True in every diagram that is consistent with the premises.

principle.text: A conclusion is valid exactly when no diagram consistent with the premises makes it false. Premises fix only what they state; every other overlap between the circles stays open.

lesson.limits: When neither a conclusion nor its contradictory follows, the options may still offer "Either I or II". That choice is right only when the two conclusions are contradictories of each other and neither follows on its own. Two "Some" premises give no definite link between the outer groups. The wording "All X are not Y" usually means "No X is Y", which is the contradictory of "Some X are Y": exactly one of the two is true, so a question offering both as conclusions points to "Either I or II" when neither follows alone.

example.problem: Premises: Some artists are bakers. All bakers are cooks. Does "Some artists are cooks" follow? Does "All artists are cooks" follow?
steps: Draw the bakers inside the cooks. Some artists sit inside the bakers, so they also sit inside the cooks.
Those artists are cooks, so "Some artists are cooks" holds in every allowed picture.
The premises say nothing about the other artists, who may lie outside the cooks. One such picture breaks "All artists are cooks".
example.result: "Some artists are cooks" follows; "All artists are cooks" does not.

misconceptions: Two "Some" premises, such as Some A are B and Some B are C, do not link A and C. The B members shared with A and with C can be different members.
Failing to see a conclusion in the obvious picture does not make it invalid. Test it against the most awkward allowed picture instead.

recall.q: When does a conclusion follow from the premises?
recall.a: When it is true in every diagram that is consistent with the premises.

recall.q: When is the answer "Either I or II follows"?
recall.a: When neither conclusion follows alone and the two are contradictories, so one of them must be true.

practice.stem: Premises: All lamps are devices. No device is silent. Conclusion I: No lamp is silent. Conclusion II: Some lamps are silent. Which option is correct?
practice.explanation: Every lamp is inside the devices, and the devices do not overlap the silent things, so no lamp is silent. Conclusion I follows in every picture and II fails in every picture. "Either I or II" tempts because the two are contradictories, but that option is for cases where neither follows by itself, and here I already does.

lesson.summary: Test a conclusion against every picture the premises allow. It follows only if none breaks it, and the either-or option applies only to contradictories when neither follows alone.

topics.title: Conversion, obversion and contraposition
points: Conversion swaps subject and predicate. It is valid for E (No S is P gives No P is S) and I (Some S are P gives Some P are S); A converts only to the weaker "Some P are S"; O does not convert.
Obversion changes the quality and negates the predicate: All S are P becomes No S is non-P; Some S are P becomes Some S are not non-P. It is valid for all four forms.
Contraposition swaps and negates both terms: All S are P becomes All non-P are non-S. It is valid for A and O, not for E or I.
Example: from "All engineers are graduates" you may infer "All non-graduates are non-engineers" and "Some graduates are engineers", but not "All graduates are engineers".

lesson.why: Many reasoning questions ask which restated sentence must also be true. Knowing which rewrites are safe and which only look safe separates a correct pick from the tempting wrong one.
lesson.intro: An immediate inference builds a new statement from a single given statement, with no second premise. Each of the three moves below rewrites one of the four forms "All S are P", "No S is P", "Some S are P" and "Some S are not P". Some rewrites always hold, and others hold only for certain forms. A bare rewrite that sounds natural in English is often not one of the safe ones.

definitions.meaning: Swap the subject and the predicate: "All S are P" becomes a statement about P and S.
Flip the statement between affirming and denying, and replace the predicate by its complement (non-P).
Swap the two terms and replace each by its complement: "All S are P" becomes "All non-P are non-S".

principle.text: Conversion is valid for No and Some. All converts only to the weaker "Some P are S", and Some-not does not convert. Obversion is valid for all four forms. Contraposition is valid for All and Some-not, and fails for No and Some.
principle.tex: \text{All } S \text{ are } P \;\equiv\; \text{No } S \text{ is non-}P \;\equiv\; \text{All non-}P \text{ are non-}S

lesson.limits: These rules apply to one statement read literally. They do not combine two premises; that needs a syllogism diagram. The weaker conversion of All to Some assumes S has at least one member. An unsafe rewrite is not necessarily false; it is just not forced by the given statement.

example.problem: Given "No reptile is warm-blooded", which of these must be true: (a) "No warm-blooded creature is a reptile", (b) "All reptiles are non-warm-blooded", (c) "All non-reptiles are warm-blooded"?
steps: The statement is the No form. Conversion is valid for No, so swapping the terms gives (a), which must be true.
Obversion changes No S is P into All S are non-P. Here that gives "All reptiles are non-warm-blooded", so (b) must be true.

Option (c) negates the subject and drops the link to the predicate. A cold-blooded fish is a non-reptile that is not warm-blooded, and the given statement does not rule that out, so (c) is not forced.
example.result: (a) and (b) must be true; (c) is not forced.

misconceptions: "All S are P" does not convert to "All P are S". All engineers are graduates does not make every graduate an engineer; only "Some graduates are engineers" follows.
The contrapositive is not the same as the converse or the inverse. Only the swap together with negating both terms gives an equivalent statement for All.

recall.q: Which of the four forms convert validly?
recall.a: No and Some convert to the same form with the terms swapped. All converts only to Some, and Some-not does not convert.

recall.q: What is the contrapositive of "All S are P"?
recall.a: "All non-P are non-S". It is equivalent to the original statement.

recall.q: Which of the three moves is valid for all four forms?
recall.a: Obversion. It flips the quality and negates the predicate.

practice.stem: "All pilots are trained" is given. Which statement must be true?
options: No trained person is a pilot.
practice.explanation: This is the contrapositive of the All form: swap the terms and negate both, giving "All non-trained are non-pilots". The first option tempts because it is the plain converse, but trained people may include non-pilots. The third option contradicts the given statement, since an untrained pilot would break it.

lesson.summary: Conversion works for No and Some, contraposition for All and Some-not, and obversion for every form. All converts only to Some.

topics.title: Conditional statements and their equivalents
points: "If P then Q" (P → Q) is equivalent only to its contrapositive "If not Q then not P". Its converse Q → P and inverse ¬P → ¬Q are equivalent to each other but not to the original.
Affirming the consequent (Q is true, so P) and denying the antecedent (P is false, so not Q) are the two classic invalid deductions; GATE options are built from them.
"P only if Q" means P → Q: Q is necessary for P. "P if Q" means Q → P. "P unless Q" means ¬Q → P, the same as P ∨ Q.
P → Q is false only when P is true and Q is false, so it is equivalent to ¬P ∨ Q. Its negation is P ∧ ¬Q, not "If P then not Q".
Example: "If it rains, the match is cancelled" licenses only "If the match is not cancelled, it did not rain". Seeing a cancelled match says nothing about rain.

lesson.why: Statements of the form "if this, then that" appear in GATE logic questions, and the options are built to tempt you into the invalid reversal.
lesson.intro: A conditional statement says that whenever the first part (the condition) holds, the second part (the result) holds too. It promises nothing in the other direction: the result may hold for other reasons. The only way the promise is broken is a case where the condition holds and the result fails.

definitions.meaning: The statement with both parts reversed and negated: from "if P then Q" to "if not Q then not P".
The statement with its parts swapped: from "if P then Q" to "if Q then P". It is not equivalent.

principle.text: "If P then Q" is equivalent to its contrapositive and to "not P or Q". It does not imply its converse "if Q then P" or its inverse "if not P then not Q". The phrase "P only if Q" also means "if P then Q".

lesson.limits: This is the logic of a single one-way promise. A sentence that says "if and only if" gives both directions, so the converse then holds too. Everyday speech often means "if and only if" when it says "if", but GATE questions say "based only on this statement" and expect the one-way reading.

example.problem: The rule is: "If the server is down, the page shows an error." The page shows no error. What follows about the server?
steps: Write P as "the server is down" and Q as "the page shows an error". The rule is P → Q.
The page shows no error, so Q is false.
The contrapositive is: if the page shows no error, the server is not down. So P is false.

misconceptions: Seeing the result does not prove the condition. An error page does not show that the server is down, because other faults could cause it.
"P only if Q" is not "if Q then P". It says Q is needed for P, which is "if P then Q".

recall.q: Which rewriting of "if P then Q" is always equivalent to it?
recall.a: The contrapositive, "if not Q then not P".

recall.q: What does "P only if Q" mean in symbols?
recall.a: P → Q: whenever P holds, Q holds, so Q is necessary for P.

practice.stem: A student passes the course only if she attends the lab. Based only on this statement, which one of the following must be true?
options: If she attends the lab, she passes the course.
If she does not attend the lab, she does not pass the course.
She attends the lab, so she passes the course.
If she does not pass the course, she did not attend the lab.
practice.explanation: "Passes only if attends" is pass → attend, whose contrapositive is: not attend → not pass. The first and third options reverse the arrow, which tempts because attendance feels like the cause of passing, but the statement only makes attendance necessary. The last option is the inverse of the statement, not-pass to not-attend, which is not forced.

lesson.summary: "If P then Q" is equivalent only to its contrapositive. The converse and the inverse are traps, and "P only if Q" means P → Q.

topics.title: Seating and ordering puzzles
points: In a straight row facing north, your left is the lower seat number. Facing south, left and right flip, so fix the facing direction before placing anyone.
Around a table with everyone facing the centre, a person's right is the next seat anticlockwise when viewed from above; with everyone facing outward it is clockwise.
Place fixed facts first (ends, exact seats), then rigid blocks ("Q immediately right of P" makes the block PQ), then negative clues ("not adjacent", "not at an end") to prune cases.
Enumerate the few surviving cases explicitly. A question is answerable only if every surviving case agrees on the asked fact; if two cases differ, a clue is still unused.
Ordering clues of the form "taller than" or "finished before" are a chain: write them as one inequality line and read off the extremes and the middle.

lesson.why: Seating and ordering puzzles are a General Aptitude question where careful case handling decides whether you reach the right arrangement.
lesson.intro: An arrangement puzzle gives a few clues about where people stand, sit or finish, and asks about one position. You place the people in the slots the clues allow. Every clue removes some arrangements, and the answer is whatever is true in all the arrangements that remain.

definitions.meaning: Two or more people that a clue ties together, such as "Q is immediately right of P", treated as one unit.
Trying each possible placement of a block or person in turn and keeping only the placements that satisfy every clue.

principle.text: Place the fixed facts first, then the blocks, then use the negative clues to prune. If several arrangements remain, the question is answerable only when they all agree on the asked fact. For a chain of order clues, write one line from smallest to largest.

lesson.limits: Left and right depend on the way people face. A person's left and right depend on the way that person faces, and seat numbers follow the direction the puzzle states. Around a table whose people face the centre, a person's left is the clockwise neighbour seen from above; if people face outward, it flips. Check which case applies before using a right or left clue.

example.problem: Four people P, Q, R and S stand in a row of four positions facing north, numbered 1 to 4 from left to right. S is at the left end. Q stands immediately to the right of P. R is not at either end. Who is at position 4?
steps: S is at position 1. P and Q form a block PQ in positions 2 to 4, so the block takes positions 2-3 or 3-4.
If the block takes 2-3, R must be at position 4, which is an end, so this case fails.
So the block takes 3-4 and R takes position 2, giving S, R, P, Q.

misconceptions: Do not stop at the first arrangement that fits. Check whether another fits, because the answer must hold in all of them.
A clue such as "X is to the right of Y" does not mean immediately right. Only "immediately" or "next to" forms a block.

recall.q: Why list the surviving cases explicitly?
recall.a: The answer is valid only if every surviving case gives the same value for the asked fact.

recall.q: In which order should clues be used?
recall.a: Fixed positions first, then blocks, then negative clues such as "not at an end".

practice.stem: Five runners A, B, C, D and E finish a race with no ties. A finishes before B. B finishes before C. D finishes before A. C finishes before E. Who finishes third?
practice.explanation: The clues chain into one line: D, A, B, C, E from first to last, so the order is fixed and the third runner is B. A tempts because it is named first in the clues, and C because it sits in the middle of the clue list, but position in the clue list says nothing about finishing position.

lesson.summary: Fix what is certain, tie blocks together, prune with negative clues, and trust the answer only when all surviving arrangements agree.

topics.title: Truth-teller and liar puzzles
points: Assume each candidate scenario in turn (who is guilty, who is the liar), evaluate every statement under that assumption, and keep only scenarios that match the stated count of true statements.
Look for two statements that contradict each other: exactly one of them is true, which uses up the truth budget fast when "exactly one statement is true".
A statement about another statement ("B is lying") has the opposite truth value of that statement, so the two always split one true, one false.
With n suspects and one culprit, there are only n cases. A 4-row table of statement truth values settles the puzzle in under two minutes.

lesson.why: Statement-checking puzzles reward a fixed method, and each one is decided by trying the few possible culprits and counting true statements.
lesson.intro: In these puzzles several people make statements and you are told how many are true, for example exactly one or exactly two. You do not guess who is lying. Instead you suppose each person is the culprit in turn, work out which statements would then be true, and keep the case whose count matches.

definitions.meaning: The stated number of true statements. Every case must use exactly that many.
Evaluating every statement under one assumption and comparing the count of true ones with the budget.

principle.text: With n suspects there are n cases. Evaluate all statements in each case and keep the case whose true-statement count equals the budget. Two statements that contradict each other always give exactly one true and one false.

lesson.limits: The method needs the budget and the number of culprits to be stated. If the puzzle only says each person is a knight or a liar without a budget, you test each person's claim for self-consistency instead of counting. When every statement or label is known to be false, use that falsity to eliminate cases. In the three mislabelled boxes puzzle, every label is wrong, so the box labelled with the mixture cannot hold the mixture and must be a pure box.

example.problem: Exactly one of A, B and C did it, and exactly one statement is true. A says "B did it". B says "I did not do it". C says "A is lying". Who did it?
steps: A and B contradict each other, so exactly one of them is true. That uses the whole budget of one true statement.
So C's statement is false, which means A is not lying and A's statement is true.
A's statement says B did it. Check: A is true, B ("I did not do it") is false, C is false, which is one true statement.
example.result: B did it, and only B's case gives exactly one true statement.

misconceptions: A statement that is false does not tell you the opposite of what it says about everyone. It only says its own claim fails.
Counting the true statements for one case is not enough. Check the remaining cases too, since a unique answer needs every other case to fail.

recall.q: What do you do with two contradicting statements?
recall.a: Exactly one of them is true, so they use one unit of the truth budget between them.

recall.q: How many cases does a puzzle with n suspects and one culprit have?
recall.a: n cases, one per suspect, each checked against the stated number of true statements.

practice.stem: Three witnesses speak about suspects X, Y and Z, and exactly one of the three did it. Witness 1 says "X did it". Witness 2 says "Z did it". Witness 3 says "Z did not do it". Exactly two of the statements are true. Who did it?
practice.explanation: Statements 2 and 3 contradict each other, so exactly one is true. The budget is two, so statement 1 must be true and X did it. Checking: if Y did it, only statement 3 is true, and if Z did it, only statement 2 is true. Z tempts because two of the three statements name it, but its count of true statements is one.

lesson.summary: Try each suspect, count the true statements, and keep the case that matches the budget. Contradicting statements always spend exactly one true.

topics.title: Blood relations and family trees
points: Parse a chained description from the speaker outward: "my mother's only son" is the speaker if the speaker is male, otherwise the speaker's brother.
Draw the tree: males as squares, females as circles, a single horizontal line for siblings, a double line for a married couple, and a vertical line for parent and child.
Count generations vertically. Two levels up on the mother's side is maternal grandparent; a parent's sibling is uncle or aunt; a sibling's child is nephew or niece.
Gender comes only from words like he, she, son, mother, brother. A name alone never fixes gender, so a relation that depends on it may be undetermined.
Coded relations ("A * B means A is the father of B") are decoded one operator at a time from left to right, each operator linking adjacent names.

lesson.why: Relation puzzles are short, but one misread link flips the answer, so a fixed way of reading the chain saves marks.
lesson.intro: A blood-relation puzzle describes people through chains such as "my father's only brother's daughter". You resolve the chain one link at a time, starting from the speaker, and name the final person's relation to the speaker. Sketching a small tree with one generation per row keeps the links straight.

definitions.meaning: One level of the tree: siblings and cousins share a level, and parents sit one level up.
A puzzle that defines symbols for relations, such as P # Q meaning P is the father of Q, and asks you to decode a chain of them.

principle.text: Resolve the chain from the speaker outward, one link at a time, and record gender only where a word fixes it. A name alone never fixes gender. In coded relations, each symbol joins two adjacent names and is read from left to right.

lesson.limits: If a relation depends on a gender the text never states, such as the sex of a child described only by name, the answer is undetermined. Do not guess a gender to force an answer.

example.problem: P # Q means P is the father of Q. P @ Q means P is the sister of Q. In M @ N # O, how is M related to O?
steps: M @ N means M is the sister of N, so M is female and shares parents with N.
N # O means N is the father of O.
M is the sister of O's father.

misconceptions: A cousin is not a sibling. A father's brother's daughter has different parents from the speaker, so she is a cousin even though she stands in the speaker's own generation.
"Only" matters. "My mother's only brother" names one person, but "my mother's brother" may name several.

recall.q: Where do you start when you resolve a chain of relations?
recall.a: At the speaker, resolving one link at a time outward.

recall.q: Does a name alone tell you a person's gender?
recall.a: No. Only words such as she, son or mother fix gender.

practice.stem: Pointing at a woman, Kiran says: "She is the daughter of my father's only brother." How is the woman related to Kiran?
practice.explanation: Kiran's father's brother is Kiran's uncle, and his daughter is the uncle's child, so she is Kiran's cousin. Sister tempts because she is in Kiran's generation, but a sister would share Kiran's own father, not his father's brother.

lesson.summary: Resolve each link from the speaker outward, and let only explicit gender words fix gender. A parent's sibling's child is a cousin.

topics.title: Direction sense and distance
points: North is up, east right, south down, west left; N → E → S → W is clockwise. A right turn is 90° clockwise, a left turn 90° anticlockwise.
Track position as coordinates (x east, y north). Each leg adds to x or y; the straight-line distance from the start is √(x² + y²).
Net heading after turns: add clockwise angles, subtract anticlockwise ones, reduce mod 360°. Facing north, 135° clockwise then 45° anticlockwise leaves a net 90° clockwise: east.
"Direction of the start with respect to the end" is the reverse vector of "end with respect to the start": north-east becomes south-west.
Shadows: in the morning the sun is in the east, so shadows fall west; in the evening they fall east. At noon shadows are negligible.

lesson.why: Direction questions give a trail of turns and ask where you end up. They are short and fully mechanical, so every mark depends only on keeping a clean record of the position.
lesson.intro: A direction problem describes a person who walks some distance, turns, and walks again. Treat the start as the point (0, 0), with east as the positive x axis and north as the positive y axis. Each leg changes one coordinate: east adds to x, west subtracts from x, north adds to y, south subtracts from y. After the last leg the coordinates tell you how far and in which direction the person is from the start. A map works the same way. Put a reference point such as a crossing at (0, 0) and read each place as an offset: right of it is east and above it is north. A place that is both right and above the reference is to its north-east.

definitions.meaning: The straight line from the start point to the end point, which ignores the winding path between them.
The compass direction the person currently faces. A right turn moves it 90 degrees clockwise and a left turn 90 degrees anticlockwise.

principle.text: Add up the east-west legs to get x and the north-south legs to get y. The distance from the start is the length of the vector (x, y), and the direction of the start from the end is the opposite of the direction of the end from the start. For a map, compare the east-west offset and the north-south offset of two places separately; if both differ the direction is a corner such as south-east, and if only one differs it is a pure direction.

lesson.limits: This works only when every leg runs along one of the four compass directions. A turn of 45 degrees or a leg described by an angle must be split into components first. A right turn is relative to the current heading, so it means east only for someone who is facing north. A drawn compass may be rotated. Read north from the compass arms and not from the top of the page, and name each side by the two arms it lies between.

example.problem: A person faces north, walks 3 km, turns left and walks 4 km. How far is she from the start, and in which direction is the start from her?
steps: Facing north, she walks 3 km: the position is $(0, 3)$.
A left turn from north points west, so the 4 km leg subtracts from $x$: the position is $(-4, 3)$.
The distance is $\sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5$ km.
She is 4 km west and 3 km north of the start, so the start lies 4 km east and 3 km south of her: south-east.
example.result: She is 5 km from the start, and the start is to her south-east.

misconceptions: Adding all the leg lengths gives the distance walked, not the distance from the start. The question usually asks for the second one.
A right turn does not always mean east. After walking west, a right turn points north; always turn relative to the current heading.
The direction of the start from the end is the reverse of the direction of the end from the start, so a north-east answer must be flipped to south-west when the question asks it the other way round.
Two places in the same row of a map differ only east-west, so one is due west of the other, not north-west. A corner direction needs a difference in both offsets.

recall.q: After facing south, which compass direction does a left turn give?
recall.a: East. Facing south, a left turn is 90 degrees anticlockwise from south, which is east.

recall.q: How do you find the straight-line distance after a walk along compass directions?
recall.a: Sum the east-west legs and the north-south legs separately, then take the square root of the sum of their squares.

recall.q: Why can the distance from the start be shorter than the distance walked?
recall.a: Legs in opposite directions cancel in the coordinates, but both count fully in the distance walked.

recall.q: On a map, a library is 2 km west and 1 km south of a crossing, and a lab is 3 km east and 2 km north of it. In which direction is the lab from the library?
recall.a: North-east. The lab is 5 km east and 3 km north of the library, so both offsets differ.

practice.stem: A person starts at a point and walks 10 km east, then 14 km north, then 4 km west, then 6 km south. How far, in km, is she from the starting point?
practice.explanation: East and west legs give $x = 10 - 4 = 6$, and north and south legs give $y = 14 - 6 = 8$. The distance is $\sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = 10$ km. The total walked is 34 km and tempts those who add every leg; the sum of the net legs, $6 + 8 = 14$, also tempts those who forget the square root.

lesson.summary: Keep a running (x, y) with east and north positive, update one coordinate per leg, and finish with the square root of x squared plus y squared. Reverse the vector when the question asks the direction of the start.

topics.title: Number series and inductive patterns
points: Test in order: first differences, second differences, ratios, then squares and cubes nearby (n² ± k, n³ ± k), primes, and finally two interleaved series on alternate positions.
A constant second difference means a quadratic term rule. For 3, 8, 17, 30, 47 the differences 5, 9, 13, 17 rise by 4, so the next difference is 21 and the next term 68.
Mixed rules "multiply then add" grow roughly geometrically: 5, 11, 23, 47 follows ×2 + 1, so the next term is 95.
Alternating patterns: 1, 4, 27, 16, 125, 36 is n³ for odd n and n² for even n, so the 7th term is 7³ = 343.
Missing-term and wrong-term variants use the same tests; the wrong term is the one that breaks an otherwise clean difference or ratio table.

lesson.why: A missing-term series is a short question whose answer is a single number, so it rewards a fixed order of tests more than flashes of insight.
lesson.intro: A number series is a list of numbers produced by one rule that turns each term into the next. Your job is to find that rule from the terms you can see, then use it on the gap. Start by writing the gap between each pair of neighbours. If those gaps are all equal, the rule is simply adding that amount. If they are not, look at how the gaps themselves change.

definitions.meaning: A term minus the term just before it.
The difference between two neighbouring first differences.

principle.text: Test in a fixed order: first differences, then second differences, then ratios, then nearby squares and cubes, then two interleaved series. A constant second difference means the terms follow a quadratic rule, so the next first difference is the last one plus that constant. A single wrong term shows up as the one term that breaks an otherwise clean difference or ratio pattern. When terms carry letter labels, such as P, Q, R, S, T, use the labels to place the given terms: if P = 3, R = 27 and T = 243, the ratio over two steps is 9, so each step multiplies by 3 and Q = 9 and S = 81.

lesson.limits: A finite list fits many rules, so the rule you find is the intended one only when it is simple and fits every given term. When two rules fit, prefer the simpler one. A rule that needs a special exception for one term is almost always wrong.

steps: The first differences are 3, 5, 7, 9; they are not constant.
The second differences are all 2, so each difference grows by 2.
The next first difference is 9 + 2 = 11.
The next term is 28 + 11 = 39.

misconceptions: Spotting a pattern in the first three terms and stopping is risky. Check the rule against every given term before using it.
A series that grows quickly is not always a product rule. Differences that double, such as 2, 4, 8, point to a power of 2 plus a constant, not to repeated multiplication of the terms.
If the differences look random, try two interleaved series on alternate positions before giving up.

recall.q: What does a constant second difference tell you?
recall.a: The terms follow a quadratic rule, and the first differences rise or fall by that constant each step.

recall.q: In what order should you test a series?
recall.a: First differences, second differences, ratios, nearby squares and cubes, and finally two interleaved series.

recall.q: How do you spot the wrong term in a series with one error?
recall.a: It is the term that breaks an otherwise clean difference or ratio pattern.

practice.stem: What is the next term of the series 3, 5, 9, 17, ?
practice.explanation: The first differences are 2, 4, 8, and they double each time, so the next difference is 16 and the next term is 17 + 16 = 33. Each term is also $2^n + 1$, which gives $2^5 + 1 = 33$. Adding 8 again gives 25, which tempts those who repeat the last difference instead of continuing its pattern. The value 31 would need a last difference of 14, which continues no simple pattern of 2, 4, 8, so the doubling rule is preferred.

lesson.summary: Write the first differences, then the second differences, then ratios, and extend the pattern that is constant. Confirm the rule on every given term before you trust it.

topics.title: Letter series and coding–decoding
points: Letter positions A = 1 … Z = 26. The anchors E = 5, J = 10, O = 15, T = 20, Y = 25 (EJOTY) locate any letter in one or two steps.
Reverse-alphabet (mirror) coding pairs each letter with the one whose position adds to 27: A with Z, G with T, M with N.
Shift codes add a fixed or growing offset to each position, wrapping past Z (Y + 3 = B). Check the first two letters to find the offset, then confirm on the rest.
Value codes map a word to a number, usually the sum of letter positions: CAT = 3 + 1 + 20 = 24, DOG = 4 + 15 + 7 = 26, so RAT = 18 + 1 + 20 = 39.
Letter series use the same difference tests as numbers on the positions, often with two interleaved sequences.

lesson.why: Coding questions turn a few letters into a fixed rule and ask you to apply it to a new word, so the whole question is finding the rule from the first pair of letters.
lesson.intro: In a letter code, the same rule changes every letter of a word. To work with the rule you convert letters into their positions in the alphabet, A as 1 up to Z as 26, and compare the original position with the coded position. If every letter moves by the same amount, the rule is a shift. If the positions of a letter and its code always add to the same number, the rule is a mirror, where A swaps with Z, B with Y, and so on.

definitions.meaning: Every letter moves forward or backward by the same number of places, wrapping from Z back to A.
Each letter is replaced by the letter at the same distance from the other end of the alphabet, so positions add to 27.

principle.text: Find the rule on the first letter or two, confirm it on the rest of the word, and then apply it to the new word. For a shift of $k$ the coded position is the original plus $k$ reduced mod 26; for a mirror it is 27 minus the original. If a code is a reversal plus a shift, the first letter of the code is the last letter of the word moved by the shift. Reverse the word, then shift each letter.

lesson.limits: Some codes combine two steps, such as reversing the whole word and then shifting. Detect this by comparing the ends: for IMAGE written as FHBNJ the code starts with F, which is E (the last letter) plus 1, and ends with J, which is I (the first letter) plus 1. Reverse IMAGE to get EGAMI, then add 1 to each letter. If positions neither differ by a constant nor add to 27, check for a growing shift or a reorder before assuming the question is broken.

example.problem: In a certain code CAB is written as FDE. How is XYZ written in that code?
steps: Compare positions: C (3) to F (6), A (1) to D (4), B (2) to E (5). Each letter moves 3 places forward.
The rule is a shift of +3, so apply it to X, Y and Z.
X (24) becomes 27, which wraps past 26 to 1, so X becomes A. Y becomes B and Z becomes C.

misconceptions: Forgetting to wrap around is one slip: after Z the count goes back to A, so X plus 3 is A and not a symbol beyond the alphabet.
Checking only the first letter is not enough. A single letter can fit a shift and a mirror at once, so confirm on at least a second letter.
A mirror pairs positions that add to 27, not 26. A is 1 and Z is 26, which sum to 27.

recall.q: Which letter does a mirror code give for G?
recall.a: T. G is position 7, and 27 minus 7 is 20, which is T.

recall.q: How do you recognise a shift code?
recall.a: Every letter's coded position differs from its original by the same amount, wrapping past Z.

recall.q: Why check a second letter after finding a rule?
recall.a: One letter can fit more than one rule, and the second letter shows which rule is the real one.

recall.q: How can you tell that a code reverses the word and then shifts it?
recall.a: The first letter of the code matches the last letter of the word moved by some shift, and the last letter of the code matches the first letter moved by the same shift.

practice.stem: In a code, each letter is replaced by its mirror letter in the alphabet, so A becomes Z and B becomes Y. How is LOG written in that code?
practice.explanation: The positions are L = 12, O = 15, G = 7. Subtracting each from 27 gives 15, 12 and 20, which are O, L and T. MPH is LOG shifted forward by 1, and KNF is LOG shifted back by 1, so both tempt those who assume a shift without checking.

lesson.summary: Convert letters to positions, test a constant difference for a shift and a constant sum of 27 for a mirror, confirm on a second letter, and apply the rule with wrap-around.

topics.title: Word and number analogies
points: Name the relation in a full sentence before looking at options: "a chisel is the tool a sculptor uses". The correct pair fits the same sentence in the same order.
Common word relations: synonym, antonym, part to whole, cause to effect, tool to user, worker to product, degree (warm : hot), and defect to object (errata : book).
Order matters: Doctor : Hospital is worker to workplace, so Hospital : Doctor in an option breaks the analogy even though the words match.
Number analogies hide a function: 7 : 50 :: 9 : 82 is n² + 1. Try squares, cubes, n(n ± 1), digit sums and simple multiples, and confirm the rule on the given pair only.
When two options fit loosely, pick the one that matches the specific relation, not just the general topic.

lesson.why: Analogy questions test whether you can name a relation exactly. Choosing by topic instead of by relation loses marks here.
lesson.intro: An analogy such as A : B :: C : D says that A relates to B in the same way C relates to D. Read it as A is to B as C is to D. You solve it by first saying the relation of the complete pair in a full sentence, for example the first word is the tool and the second is the person who uses it. Then you fill the other pair so that the same sentence is true, with the words in the same order.

analogy.text: An analogy is a template with two slots, like a sentence frame: you learn the frame from the complete pair and fill the other pair into it.
analogy.breaksWhen: A frame that is too broad, such as the words are related, fits several options, so the sentence must be specific enough to rule options out.

definitions.meaning: The specific link between two words, such as tool to user, part to whole or cause to effect.
An option that is about the same subject as the question but does not carry the same relation.

principle.text: Write the relation of the complete pair as a sentence, then test each option in the same sentence, in the same order. The option that makes the sentence true for the second pair is the answer, even if other options share the topic.
principle.tex: A : B \;::\; C : D \iff \mathrm{rel}(A, B) = \mathrm{rel}(C, D)

lesson.limits: The method needs a relation that is stated clearly by the complete pair. If two options both fit, make the sentence more specific by adding the kind of word expected, such as an action or a place. For number analogies the relation is a function, so test it on the given pair and apply it to the other number.

example.problem: Author : Novel :: Architect : ?  Options: Engineer, Climate, Hammer, Building.
steps: State the relation: an author is the person who creates a novel, so the first word is a creator and the second is the thing created.
Apply the same sentence: an architect is the person who designs a building.
Test the options in that sentence. Engineer is another person, Hammer is a tool and Climate is not made by anyone, so only Building is a thing an architect creates.

misconceptions: Choosing the word that is simply associated with the third word is a mistake. Hospital goes with doctor, but if the pair is a tool and its user then a place is wrong.
Order matters. Doctor : Hospital is worker to workplace, so Hospital : Doctor breaks the analogy even though the words are the same.
Two pairs of the same kind of word are not enough. Both pairs must carry the same specific relation, not merely both be places or both be people.

recall.q: What is the first step in solving A : B :: C : D?
recall.a: State the relation of the complete pair A and B in a full sentence.

recall.q: Why does the order of words in an option matter?
recall.a: The relation has a direction, so reversing the pair changes it into a different relation.

recall.q: What rule links 7 : 50 and 9 : 82?
recall.a: Each number is squared and 1 is added, since 7 squared plus 1 is 50 and 9 squared plus 1 is 82.

practice.explanation: A hammer is the tool a carpenter uses, so the blank is the person who uses a scalpel: a surgeon. Hospital is a place and Sharp is a quality of the tool, so neither names the user. Operation tempts because a scalpel is used in one, but that is the task, not the user.

lesson.summary: Turn the complete pair into a one-sentence relation, keep the order of the words, and pick the option that fits the same sentence, not the one that merely shares the subject.

topics.title: Odd one out and matrix completion
points: Odd one out: find the property shared by all but one item, such as primality, perfect powers, word category or letter-gap pattern. Check that the rule excludes exactly one option.
Example: in 37, 41, 51, 53 only 51 = 3 × 17 is composite, so 51 is the odd one.
Matrix completion: rows or columns obey a rule (sum, product, or one figure transformed step by step). Find it on a complete row, verify on a second, then apply to the gap.
If two rules fit the complete rows, the one that also fits the columns is intended.

lesson.why: These questions look like guessing games but have one hidden rule. A fixed method of counting or testing exposes the rule quickly.
lesson.intro: In an odd-one-out question, all items but one share a property and the odd one lacks it. In a matrix-completion question, a grid of figures or numbers follows a rule along its rows or columns, and one cell is missing. In both cases you are searching for a rule. You test simple properties first, such as whether a number is prime, a perfect square or a multiple, and for a grid you compute a number from each cell, such as a count, a sum or a product.

definitions.meaning: The single item that does not share the property all the others share.
Finding the missing cell of a grid so that every row or column obeys the same rule.

principle.text: Find the rule on a complete row or on the items that clearly agree, then check it on a second row or on all the other items. A rule is right only if it picks out exactly one odd item, or fits every complete row of the grid and the column test if rows alone are ambiguous.

lesson.limits: If two different rules both fit the complete rows, the one that also fits the columns is the intended rule. In an odd-one-out question, a property that excludes two options is not the rule. Counting-based grids can also use a global property such as a magic sum rather than a row-by-row formula. Other grids hold a count in each cell, such as dots or neighbouring cells of a given kind, so compute that count before comparing.

example.problem: Which one of 121, 144, 169, 200 is the odd one out?
steps: Look for a property that most items share. $121 = 11^2$, $144 = 12^2$ and $169 = 13^2$.
The property is being a perfect square.
$14^2 = 196$ and $15^2 = 225$, so 200 lies between two squares and is not a perfect square.

misconceptions: Picking an answer because it looks different on the page is not a test. Prove the shared property for every other item.
A rule found on one row is not yet a rule. Check it on a second row, because several rules can fit one row of three cells.
Do not treat a property that excludes two items as the answer; the odd one out must be unique.

recall.q: How do you confirm a rule in a matrix puzzle?
recall.a: Find it on a complete row, then verify it on a second row or on the columns before filling the gap.

recall.q: What if two rules fit every complete row?
recall.a: Choose the rule that also fits the columns, since the intended rule works in both directions.

recall.q: Why is 49 the odd one out of 29, 37, 49, 53?
recall.a: 29, 37 and 53 are prime, while 49 is 7 times 7, a composite number.

recall.q: A 3 by 3 grid of dot counts has rows 4, 9, 2 and 3, 5, 7, and its last row starts 8, 1. What must the last cell be if every row has the same sum?
recall.a: 6. The first row sums to 15, so the last row needs $8 + 1 + 6 = 15$.

practice.stem: In a grid of numbers, one rule links the first two numbers of a row to its third. The complete rows are 2, 3, 7 and 4, 2, 9 and 3, 4, 13. The last row is 5, 3, and a missing cell. What is the missing number?
practice.explanation: Test the first row: $2 \times 3 = 6$, one less than 7. The second row gives $4 \times 2 = 8$, one less than 9, and the third gives $3 \times 4 = 12$, one less than 13. Three rows agree, so the rule is product plus 1, and the last row gives $5 \times 3 + 1 = 16$. The bare product, 15, tempts those who stop at the first idea without checking that it fits the rows. A rule such as first number plus 5 fits the first two rows but gives 8 on the third, so the third row is what rules it out. Adding the first two numbers gives 5, 6 and 7 and fits no row.

lesson.summary: Find the rule on the agreeing items or a complete row, check it on a second row or the columns, make sure it singles out exactly one odd item, and then apply it to the gap.

topics.title: Argument structure: assumptions, conclusions, strengthen and weaken
points: An argument has premises (stated support), a conclusion (the claim) and assumptions (unstated premises the conclusion needs). Indicator words: therefore, hence, so mark conclusions; because, since mark premises.
An assumption is implicit if negating it destroys the argument (the negation test). "Advertise on TV to raise sales" assumes TV adverts reach likely buyers.
A conclusion follows only if the statement guarantees it. Options with extreme words (always, only, all, never) usually overreach.
Strengtheners add support for the link between premise and conclusion or rule out an alternative cause; weakeners supply another cause or show the premise does not lead to the result.
Course-of-action questions: an action follows if it is practical and directly addresses the stated problem.

lesson.why: Reasoning questions reward reading exactly what a passage says and nothing more. Marks are lost by accepting an option because it sounds sensible rather than because the text forces it.
lesson.intro: An argument has a conclusion, which is the claim being made, and premises, which are the stated reasons for it. Between them sits an assumption: something the argument needs but does not say. Questions ask you to find the assumption, to decide what must be true given the passage, or to say which new fact makes the argument stronger or weaker. Words such as therefore and hence mark the conclusion, and because and since mark a premise.

definitions.meaning: An unstated claim that the conclusion needs in order to follow from the premises.
Deny a candidate assumption. If the argument then falls apart, the candidate really was an assumption.
A statement that the passage forces to be true, so it cannot be false while the passage is true.

principle.text: A statement follows from a passage only if the passage cannot be true while it is false. An assumption passes the negation test. A strengthener adds support for the link between premise and conclusion or removes a rival cause; a weakener supplies a rival cause or cuts the link. A percentage of one group says nothing about a different group. Nested percentages multiply: if 90% of a group have a trait and 60% of those also have a second trait, then $0.9 \times 0.6 = 54\%$ of the group have both. Never apply a percentage to a base it was not stated for.

lesson.limits: Use only the passage. Outside knowledge, however true, does not make an inference valid. Options with extreme words such as always, only, all or never usually claim more than the text supports, though the word alone does not decide: check what the passage says about the whole group.

example.problem: A council argues: ban cars from the town centre, and air pollution there will fall. Which statement is an assumption of this argument?
steps: The conclusion is that banning cars will lower central air pollution.
Test the claim cars are a major source of pollution in the centre. Its negation is that cars are not a significant source.
If cars are not a significant source, a ban would not lower pollution, so the argument fails.
example.result: The assumption is that cars are a significant source of the pollution in the town centre.

misconceptions: An option that is true or sensible is not necessarily an assumption. It must be needed by the argument, which the negation test checks.
A statement that the passage makes likely is not an inference. It must be forced, so one allowed situation in which it fails is enough to reject it.
A weakener does not have to disprove the conclusion. It only has to make the conclusion less likely, usually by offering another cause.

recall.q: How do you test whether a statement is an assumption?
recall.a: Negate it. If the argument then falls apart, the statement was an assumption.

recall.q: When does a statement follow from a passage?
recall.a: Only when the passage cannot be true while the statement is false.

recall.q: What kind of fact weakens a cause-and-effect argument?
recall.a: Another cause that explains the effect, or evidence that the effect happened without the stated cause.

recall.q: A passage says some members of a group have a trait. Does it follow that all of them have it, or that none of the others do?
recall.a: No. Some means at least one, so it allows all and it allows only a few; an option with always or all needs the passage to say so for the whole group.

practice.stem: A shop owner says: sales rose after we introduced a loyalty card, so the card caused the rise. Which finding most weakens this claim?
options: Customers with the card visit twice as often as before.
A large factory opened nearby that month and brought thousands of new customers.
The loyalty card is free to join.
Some customers asked for a card with a different design.
practice.explanation: The claim is that the card caused the rise, so the weakener is a rival cause: the new factory customers could explain the rise without the card. Frequent visits by card holders tempt because they are relevant, but they strengthen the claim. The free card and the design requests have no bearing on what caused the rise.

lesson.summary: Separate premise from conclusion, test assumptions by negating them, accept an inference only if the passage forces it, and weaken or strengthen a cause claim through rival causes.

topics.title: Common logical fallacies
points: Ad hominem attacks the person instead of the argument ("ignore his tax proposal, he failed school").
Straw man restates an opponent's position in a weaker form and refutes that instead.
Circular reasoning puts the conclusion inside a premise ("the book is reliable because it says it is").
Formal fallacies with conditionals: affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent. False dilemma offers two options when more exist; hasty generalisation draws a rule from too few cases.

lesson.why: Critical-reasoning questions often ask which argument is flawed or which reply exposes the flaw. Naming the fallacy fast tells you which option to reject.
lesson.intro: A fallacy is an argument whose conclusion does not follow from its premises, even if the argument sounds convincing. Some fallacies break the logical form, as with an if-then statement used the wrong way round. Others sidestep the actual claim, by attacking the speaker or distorting the claim. To spot one, restate the argument as premises and a conclusion, then ask whether the premises really force it.

definitions.meaning: Attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim itself.
Replaces the opponent's position with a weaker version and refutes that version.
Uses the conclusion, in other words, as one of its own premises.
Offers two options as if they were the only ones when others exist.

principle.text: For "If P then Q", only two moves are valid: P is true so Q is true, and Q is false so P is false. Affirming the consequent (Q is true so P) and denying the antecedent (P is false so not Q) are both fallacies.
principle.tex: P \to Q,\; Q \;\nvdash\; P \qquad P \to Q,\; \lnot P \;\nvdash\; \lnot Q

lesson.limits: A fallacy makes an argument unsound, but it does not make the conclusion false. A conclusion can be true by luck while the reasoning is still faulty. Also, a claim about someone's expertise or record is not always ad hominem: it is a fallacy only when it replaces the argument.

example.problem: "If it rains, the road is wet. The road is wet. Therefore it rained." Is the argument valid?
steps: Write the premises: P is "it rains" and Q is "the road is wet". The rule is P → Q, and the fact given is Q.
The conclusion is P, so the argument goes from Q back to P. That is affirming the consequent.
A wet road has other causes, such as a washed street or a burst pipe, so Q can be true while P is false.
example.result: Invalid: it affirms the consequent, so the conclusion does not follow.

misconceptions: Treating "If P then Q" as if it also said "if Q then P". Q may have causes besides P.
Calling any criticism of a person ad hominem. It is the fallacy only when the person is attacked in place of answering the argument.

recall.q: What is the difference between ad hominem and straw man?
recall.a: Ad hominem attacks the speaker. Straw man distorts the speaker's claim into a weaker one and attacks that.

recall.q: Which two conditional moves are fallacies?
recall.a: Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent.

recall.q: What makes reasoning circular?
recall.a: The conclusion is assumed in a premise, so the argument proves nothing new.

practice.stem: "If the server is down, the page fails to load. The server is not down. So the page loads." What is wrong with this argument?
options: It attacks the person instead of the claim.
practice.explanation: The rule is P → Q with P as "server down". The argument says P is false and concludes that Q is false too, which is denying the antecedent. Affirming the consequent tempts because it is the other common conditional fallacy, but here the premise is about P, not Q. The page could fail for another reason.

lesson.summary: A fallacy breaks the link between premises and conclusion. Learn the four named informal types and the two conditional ones: affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent.

topics.title: Numerical relations: inequality chains, ranking and data sufficiency
points: Inequality chains: combine adjacent signs. A > B ≥ C gives A > C; A ≥ B ≥ C gives A ≥ C; opposite signs (A > B < C) give no relation between A and C.

Coded inequalities are decoded to ≤, ≥, <, > first, then chained. With @ = ≤, # = ≥, % = >, & = =, the clues A % B, B # C, C & D, D @ E read A > B ≥ C = D ≤ E: A > D and E ≥ C follow, but E > C and A > E do not.
Ranking in a line: total = rank from top + rank from bottom − 1. If A is 14th from the left and 23rd from the right, the row has 36 people.
People between two positions counted from opposite ends: between = N − (r₁ + r₂) when r₁ + r₂ ≤ N; if r₁ + r₂ > N + 1 the stretches overlap and the count is r₁ + r₂ − N − 2.

Data sufficiency: a statement is sufficient when every value it allows gives the same answer, and a sure "no" counts. Test I alone, II alone, then both together. Is integer x > 0? x² > 0 fails (x = 2 and x = −2 both fit); x³ > 0 settles it.

Number-property reasoning: parity, divisibility and sign rules (odd + odd = even, a product of nonzero factors is negative iff it has an odd number of negative factors) eliminate options without full computation.

lesson.why: Comparison puzzles on heights, ages or ranks appear in the General Aptitude section, and every one reduces to building a single ordered line and then counting along it.
lesson.intro: When every person differs, such as in height, they stand in exactly one order from shortest to tallest. Each clue either says who stands above whom or fixes a place in that line. A statement like "taller than only two people" means exactly two people are below that person, so it names a position. Place the clues that fix a position first, then slot in the pairwise clues, and finally count the people above or below whoever the question names.

definitions.meaning: The number of people shorter than a person, plus one.
A clue such as "X is taller than Y" that orders two people without saying where either stands.

principle.text: With n distinct values in one line, a person with k people below has n - 1 - k people above. Fix positions from clues that count people, then use pairwise clues to order the rest.

lesson.limits: This works only when all values are distinct and the clues pin down a single order. If two people may be equal, or the clues leave two orders possible, the count can change and the answer is not determined. Always check that your final line satisfies every clue.

example.problem: Five people A, B, C, D and E have different heights. I: C is shorter than B. II: D is the shortest. III: A is taller than exactly two people. IV: E is taller than B. How many people are taller than C?
steps: Clue II puts D at the bottom. Clue III says exactly two people are below A, so A is third from the bottom and D is one of those two.

Who is the second person below A? B cannot be, because C is shorter than B and would then also be below A, making three. E cannot be either, because E is taller than B, which would again pull B and C below A.
So C is the second person below A, and the line from the bottom starts D, C, A.
B and E fill the top two places, and clue IV puts E above B, so the full line is D, C, A, B, E.
The people above C are A, B and E.
example.result: Three people are taller than C.

misconceptions: Reading "taller than only one person" as "one person is taller than them" reverses the count. It means exactly one person is below, so the person is second from the bottom.
Counting the named person in the total gives an answer one too large. People taller than C do not include C, so take positions above C only.

recall.q: What does "X is taller than exactly k people" tell you?
recall.a: Exactly k people are below X, so X is in position k + 1 counting from the shortest.

recall.q: In a line of n distinct people, how many are taller than a person who has k shorter?
recall.a: n - 1 - k people are taller.

recall.q: Which clues should you place first when building the order?
recall.a: Clues that fix a position, such as the shortest, the tallest or an exact count below, before pairwise clues.

practice.stem: Five children P, Q, R, S and T have different heights. I: R is shorter than P. II: P is shorter than S. III: Q is taller than exactly one child. IV: S is shorter than T. How many children are shorter than S?
practice.explanation: Q has exactly one child below, so Q is second from the bottom, and that child must be R, who is shorter than P and cannot stand anywhere else. The order from the shortest is R, Q, P, S, T. Three children (R, Q, P) are shorter than S. Answering 4 tempts when S is counted among the shorter children, and 2 tempts when Q is placed above P.

lesson.summary: Build one line from shortest to tallest, placing count-based clues first, then count above or below the named person without counting that person.

topics.title: Number properties: divisibility, unit digits, remainders and magnitude comparison
points: Divisibility tests: by 3 or 9 when the digit sum is; by 11 when the alternating digit sum is (918082: 2 − 8 + 0 − 8 + 1 − 9 = −22); by 4 from the last two digits and by 8 from the last three.
A number is divisible by a product only through coprime factors: 12 needs 3 and 4. Divisibility by 2 and by 6 does not give 12, since 6 itself passes both tests.
Unit digits of powers repeat with a period dividing 4, so the last digit of aⁿ is that of (a mod 10)ʳ with r = ((n − 1) mod 4) + 1. For 7⁹⁵, 95 mod 4 = 3 and 7³ = 343, so the last digit is 3.
Remainders survive sums and products: (a × b) mod m = ((a mod m) × (b mod m)) mod m. 17 × 23 leaves 2 × 3 = 6, that is 1, on division by 5, and 391 mod 5 = 1 confirms it.
Counting multiples in 1…N: ⌊N/a⌋ are divisible by a, and inclusion–exclusion gives "by a or b" as ⌊N/a⌋ + ⌊N/b⌋ − ⌊N/lcm(a, b)⌋. For 3 or 5 up to 100: 33 + 20 − 6 = 47.
Compare powers on a common exponent or base: 2³⁰ = 8¹⁰ < 9¹⁰ = 3²⁰. To rank √2, ∛3 and ⁶√6, raise all to the 6th power: 8, 9 and 6, so ∛3 is largest and ⁶√6 smallest.

lesson.why: Divisibility, last digits and remainders are quick ways to answer number questions without long arithmetic. They also let you compare large powers when direct calculation is out of reach.
lesson.intro: Most questions here have a shortcut that avoids computing the full number. A divisibility test looks at the digits instead of dividing. The last digit of a power repeats in a short cycle, so you only need the exponent's position in that cycle. A remainder can be found by reducing each factor first. Powers with different bases can be compared by bringing them to the same exponent.

definitions.meaning: Two numbers with no common factor except 1, such as 3 and 4. The numbers 4 and 6 are not coprime, since both divide by 2.
The least common multiple: the smallest number that both given numbers divide. lcm(4, 6) = 12.
The sum of the digits of a number. It decides divisibility by 3 and 9.
The repeating pattern of last digits of successive powers of a number.
Count multiples of a or b as those of a, plus those of b, minus those of both.

principle.text: A number divisible by two coprime numbers is divisible by their product. The last digit of a power repeats every 4 steps, and remainders can be multiplied after reducing each factor. The multiples of a or b up to N are counted by inclusion-exclusion.
principle.tex: \#\{k \le N : a \mid k \text{ or } b \mid k\} = \left\lfloor \tfrac{N}{a} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \tfrac{N}{b} \right\rfloor - \left\lfloor \tfrac{N}{\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)} \right\rfloor

lesson.limits: Combining tests works only for coprime factors: passing the tests for 2 and 6 does not give 12. The cycle shortcut gives the last digit only. To count multiples with inclusion-exclusion you must subtract at the lcm, not at the product, when the numbers share a factor.

example.problem: Is 7248 divisible by 12, and what is the last digit of $13^{58}$?
steps: 12 = 3 × 4 with 3 and 4 coprime, so test both. The digit sum 7 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 21 is divisible by 3. The last two digits 48 are divisible by 4. So 7248 is divisible by 12.
The last digit of $13^{58}$ is that of $3^{58}$. Powers of 3 end in 3, 9, 7, 1 and repeat every 4 steps.
58 mod 4 = 2, so the last digit matches the second term of the cycle, which is 9.
example.result: 7248 is divisible by 12, and $13^{58}$ ends in 9.

misconceptions: Testing a composite divisor with two non-coprime tests. A number divisible by 2 and by 6 need not be divisible by 12.
Using the exponent directly in the cycle. When the exponent is a multiple of 4, the digit is the last of the cycle, not the first.

recall.q: Which digit tests decide divisibility by 3, 9 and 11?
recall.a: 3 and 9 use the digit sum. 11 uses the alternating digit sum.

recall.q: How do you count numbers up to N divisible by a or b?
recall.a: Add the multiples of a and of b, then subtract the multiples of lcm(a, b).

recall.q: How do you compare $2^{30}$ with $3^{20}$?
recall.a: Rewrite both with a common exponent: $8^{10}$ against $9^{10}$, so $3^{20}$ is larger.

practice.stem: How many integers from 1 to 200 are divisible by 4 or by 6?
practice.explanation: There are 50 multiples of 4 and 33 multiples of 6. The multiples of both are the multiples of lcm(4, 6) = 12, which number 16. So 50 + 33 - 16 = 67. Subtracting 8 (the count for 4 × 6 = 24) tempts but is wrong because 4 and 6 share a factor, so the overlap is at 12.

lesson.summary: Use digit tests with coprime factors, cycle positions for last digits, reduced factors for remainders, inclusion-exclusion at the lcm for counts, and a common exponent for comparing powers.

formulas.name: Straight-line distance from the start
formulas.note: Sum the legs in each axis first; never add path lengths. Opposite legs cancel.

formulas.name: Net heading after successive turns
formulas.text: θ = (θ₀ + Σ clockwise − Σ anticlockwise) mod 360°
where: starting heading measured clockwise from north
formulas.note: Right turn = +90°, left turn = −90°. A negative result gets 360° added.

formulas.name: Letter position anchors
formulas.note: Count forward or back from the nearest anchor: R = T − 2 = 18.

formulas.name: Reverse-alphabet pair
formulas.note: A pairs with Z, B with Y, M with N. A word coded by its mirror letters decodes with the same rule.

formulas.name: Contrapositive equivalence
formulas.note: The converse Q → P and the inverse ¬P → ¬Q are not equivalent to P → Q.

formulas.name: Implication as a disjunction
formulas.tex: (P \to Q) \equiv (\lnot P \lor Q), \quad \lnot(P \to Q) \equiv P \land \lnot Q
formulas.note: "P unless Q" is ¬Q → P, which is P ∨ Q.

formulas.name: Total from two-sided rank
where: rank of the same person from the other end
formulas.note: The person is counted twice, hence the −1.

formulas.name: People between two ranks from opposite ends
where: rank of the first person from one end
rank of the second person from the other end
formulas.note: Valid when r₁ + r₂ ≤ N. When r₁ + r₂ > N + 1 the stretches overlap and B = r₁ + r₂ − N − 2.

formulas.name: Last digit of a power
formulas.note: Every last digit repeats with period 1, 2 or 4, so period 4 works for all. When n is a multiple of 4 use r = 4, not r = 0.

formulas.name: Integers up to N divisible by a or b
where: least common multiple of a and b
formulas.note: Subtract multiples of the lcm, not of a × b: up to 500, multiples of 4 or 6 number 125 + 83 − 41 = 167, using lcm 12.

formulas.name: Quadratic series from constant second difference
formulas.tex: t_n = a n^2 + b n + c, \quad a = \tfrac{\Delta^2}{2}
formulas.text: tₙ = a n² + b n + c with a = Δ²/2
formulas.note: Usually faster to extend the difference table than to solve for a, b, c.

problemTypes.title: Which conclusions follow from two or three categorical statements
recipe: Translate each premise into its circle picture (inside, disjoint, overlapping).
Draw the tightest diagram, then try to falsify each conclusion with an alternative diagram.
Keep only conclusions true in every diagram; check contradictory pairs on the same two terms for an either-or answer.
problemTypes.trap: Reading "Some A are B" as "Some A are not B", or rejecting an either-or pair because neither conclusion follows alone.

problemTypes.title: Valid deduction from an if-then or only-if statement
recipe: Rewrite the statement as P → Q, translating "only if", "unless" and "necessary" carefully.
Mark the contrapositive ¬Q → ¬P as the only equivalent form.
Reject options that affirm the consequent or deny the antecedent.
problemTypes.trap: Choosing the converse because it sounds natural in English.

problemTypes.title: Seating or ordering puzzle with five to eight people
recipe: Fix the frame: row or circle, facing direction, seat numbering.
Place absolute clues first, then rigid blocks, then branch on the remaining positions.
Apply negative clues to prune each branch and confirm that the asked fact is the same in every surviving case.
problemTypes.trap: Treating "to the right of" as "immediately to the right of", or mixing up left and right for people facing south or facing the centre.

problemTypes.title: Who is lying or who is guilty, with a stated number of true statements
recipe: List the candidate scenarios (one per suspect or per liar).
For each scenario, mark every statement true or false.
Keep the scenario whose count of true statements matches the condition.
problemTypes.trap: Stopping at the first scenario that looks consistent without checking the others for uniqueness.

problemTypes.title: Next or missing term of a number or letter series
recipe: Write first differences; if irregular, write second differences and ratios.
Check squares, cubes and primes near the terms, and split into alternate-position series.
Confirm the rule on every given term before computing the answer.
problemTypes.trap: Fitting a rule to the first three terms only; a rule that fails on the fourth term is wrong.

problemTypes.title: Blood-relation chain or walking-path puzzle
recipe: Blood relations: decode from the speaker outward and draw the tree with gender marks.
Directions: track (x, y) after each leg and the current heading after each turn.
Read the question's reference point before answering: relation of A to B, or direction of start from end.
problemTypes.trap: Answering the inverse relation (son instead of father) or the reverse direction.

problemTypes.title: Choose the pair with the same relation
recipe: Express the given pair as a sentence that names the relation and its direction.
Test each option in the same sentence, in the same order.
If several fit, tighten the sentence until one remains.
problemTypes.trap: Picking a pair from the same subject area whose relation differs or runs in reverse.

problemTypes.title: Inequality chain, coded inequality or data sufficiency: what is forced
recipe: Decode every symbol to ≤, ≥, <, > or = and write the clues as one chain.
For a relation between two terms, follow the chain between them: all signs the same way give the relation (strict if any sign is strict); a reversal gives none.
For data sufficiency, test I alone, II alone, then both, each time looking for two allowed values with different answers.
problemTypes.trap: Treating a statement that always answers "no" as insufficient, or reading ≥ in the chain as > when an option asks for a strict relation.

problemTypes.title: Last digit, remainder or divisibility of a large expression
recipe: Reduce every base to its last digit, or to its remainder mod m.
Reduce each exponent mod 4, replacing 0 by 4, and read the last digit from the cycle.
Add or multiply the reduced values and reduce once more.
problemTypes.trap: Using r = 0 for an exponent that is a multiple of 4, which gives 1 instead of the true last digit (2⁸ ends in 6, not 1).

problemTypes.title: Statement with assumptions, conclusions or a weakening fact
recipe: Identify the conclusion or recommended action in the statement.
For an assumption, negate each option and see whether the statement collapses.
For a conclusion, accept only what the statement guarantees, rejecting extreme wording.
problemTypes.trap: Choosing an option that is true in the real world but not needed by the argument.

questions.stem: Statements: Some cats are dogs. All dogs are rats. Which of the following conclusions follow?
questions.explanation: The cats that are dogs lie inside the dog circle, which lies inside the rat circle, so at least one cat is a rat: option 1 follows, and converting it gives "Some rats are cats" (option 3). A diagram with part of the cat circle outside rats is consistent, so "All cats are rats" fails. The dog circle may fill the whole rat circle (dogs = rats), so "Some rats are not dogs" is not forced.

questions.stem: Statements: Some tables are chairs. No chair is a desk. Which conclusion follows?
questions.explanation: The tables that are chairs sit inside the chair circle, which is disjoint from desks, so those tables are not desks: "Some tables are not desks" holds in every diagram. Tables outside the chair circle may still overlap desks, so "No table is a desk" fails. All desks could be tables (lying in the table-only region), so option 3 fails, and chairs may extend beyond tables, so option 4 fails.

questions.stem: Statements: Some books are pens. Some pens are pencils. Conclusions: I. Some books are pencils. II. No book is a pencil. Which option is correct?
questions.explanation: Both premises are particular, so the book–pen overlap and the pen–pencil overlap may or may not share members. One diagram has books and pencils overlapping (I true, II false), another keeps them apart (I false, II true), so neither follows alone. I and II are contradictories about the same two terms, so in every diagram exactly one of them is true: either I or II follows.

questions.stem: Statement: "If it rains, the match is cancelled." Which of the following is a logically valid deduction from it?
options: If the match is not cancelled, it did not rain.
If the match is cancelled, it rained.
If it does not rain, the match is not cancelled.
The match is cancelled only if it rains.
questions.explanation: Write the statement as R → C. Its only equivalent is the contrapositive ¬C → ¬R, option 1. Option 2 is the converse C → R (affirming the consequent), option 3 is the inverse ¬R → ¬C (denying the antecedent), and option 4, "C only if R", is again C → R.

questions.stem: Rule: "A visitor may enter the hall only if the visitor has a ticket." Which of the following say exactly the same thing as the rule?
options: If a visitor enters the hall, the visitor has a ticket.
If a visitor has no ticket, the visitor does not enter the hall.
If a visitor has a ticket, the visitor enters the hall.
Either the visitor has a ticket or the visitor does not enter the hall.
