questions.explanation: "E only if T" is E → T. Option 1 is E → T itself. Option 2 is the contrapositive ¬T → ¬E. Option 4 is T ∨ ¬E, which is ¬E ∨ T, the disjunctive form of E → T. Option 3 is the converse T → E: a ticket is necessary, not sufficient, so it is not equivalent. A truth table over the four (E, T) cases confirms options 1, 2 and 4 match E → T row for row and option 3 differs when E is false and T is true.

questions.stem: In a code, "A * B" means A is the father of B and "A + B" means A is the mother of B. What does "P * Q + R" mean?
options: P is the paternal grandfather of R.
P is the maternal grandfather of R.
P is the father of R.
P is the maternal uncle of R.
questions.explanation: P * Q: P is the father of Q. Q + R: Q is the mother of R, so Q is female. P is the father of R's mother, which makes P the maternal grandfather of R.

questions.stem: Starting at point O, Asha walks 10 km north, turns right and walks 6 km, turns right and walks 18 km, then turns left and walks 9 km. What is her straight-line distance from O, in km?
questions.explanation: Take east as x and north as y. North 10: (0, 10). Right turn faces east, 6 km: (6, 10). Right turn faces south, 18 km: (6, −8). Left turn from south faces east, 9 km: (15, −8). Distance = √(15² + 8²) = √289 = 17 km.

questions.stem: Ravi walks 4 km east, turns left and walks 3 km. In which direction is his starting point from where he now stands?
questions.explanation: He ends at (4, 3) relative to the start, i.e. north-east of it. The question asks for the start relative to the end, the reverse vector (−4, −3): south-west. North-east is the trap answer for the opposite question.

questions.stem: Find the next term of the series 1, 4, 27, 16, 125, 36, ?
questions.explanation: The terms are 1³, 2², 3³, 4², 5³, 6²: odd positions are cubes and even positions squares of the position number. The 7th term is 7³ = 343.

questions.stem: In a code, CAT is written as 24 and DOG as 26. Using the same rule, what number is RAT written as?
questions.explanation: Each word maps to the sum of its letter positions: C + A + T = 3 + 1 + 20 = 24 and D + O + G = 4 + 15 + 7 = 26. Then R + A + T = 18 + 1 + 20 = 39.
50 = 7² + 1, so the rule is n² + 1 and 9 maps to 81 + 1 = 82. 81 forgets the +1, 80 applies −1, and 90 = 9 × 10 uses n(n + 1), which gives 56 for 7 and does not fit the given pair.

questions.stem: Select the word that completes the analogy. Sculptor : Chisel :: Surgeon : ?
questions.explanation: The relation is worker to the tool the worker uses: a sculptor shapes with a chisel, a surgeon cuts with a scalpel. Hospital is the workplace, patient the person served and operation the activity, each a different relation.

questions.stem: Exactly one of four suspects A, B, C and D stole a laptop. A says "B did it." B says "D did it." C says "I did not do it." D says "B is lying." Exactly one of the four statements is true. Who stole the laptop?
questions.explanation: Test each suspect as the thief and count true statements. A: C's and D's statements are true, 2. B: A's, C's and D's are true, 3. C: only D's statement ("B is lying") is true, 1. D: B's and C's are true, 2. Only the case "C is the thief" gives exactly one true statement.

questions.stem: P, Q, R, S and T sit in a row of five seats, numbered 1 to 5 from left to right, all facing north. R sits at one end. Q sits immediately to the right of P. T sits immediately to the left of S. T does not sit at an end. Neither P nor S sits next to R. Who sits in the middle seat?
questions.explanation: The blocks PQ and TS plus R fill all five seats. If R is in seat 1, the blocks fill seats 2–5 as PQTS (P beside R, rejected) or TSPQ, giving R T S P Q, which passes every clue. If R is in seat 5, the blocks fill seats 1–4 as PQTS (S beside R, rejected) or TSPQ (T at an end, rejected). The unique arrangement is R T S P Q, so S is in the middle.

questions.stem: Given P > Q ≥ R = S < T, which of the following must be true?
questions.explanation: P > Q ≥ R and R = S give P > S. Q ≥ R = S gives Q ≥ S. S < T and R = S give T > R. P and T are linked only through S with opposite signs (P > S < T), so P > T is not forced: P = 2, Q = 1, R = S = 0, T = 5 satisfies the chain with P < T.

questions.stem: In a row of students, Meera is 14th from the left end and 23rd from the right end. How many students are in the row?
questions.explanation: Meera is counted in both ranks, so the total is 14 + 23 − 1 = 36.

questions.stem: P @ Q means P is not greater than Q, P # Q means P is not less than Q, P % Q means P is greater than Q, and P & Q means P equals Q. Given A % B, B # C, C & D and D @ E, which conclusion definitely follows?
questions.explanation: Decode: @ is ≤, # is ≥, % is > and & is =, so the clues read A > B ≥ C = D ≤ E. From A to D the signs all point the same way and one is strict, so A > D, which is A % D. A and E are joined through D with opposite signs, so A % E is not forced. E and C are joined by C = D ≤ E, giving only E ≥ C, so E % C fails when E = D. B ≥ C = D gives only B ≥ D, so B % D fails when B = C.

questions.stem: Is the integer n divisible by 6? Statement I: n is divisible by 3. Statement II: n² is divisible by 4. Which option is correct?
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is.
The two statements together are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: I alone allows n = 3 (no) and n = 6 (yes), so it is insufficient. If n were odd, n² would be odd, so II says exactly that n is even; it allows n = 2 (no) and n = 6 (yes), so it is insufficient. Together, n is divisible by the coprime factors 2 and 3, hence by 6, and the answer is always yes.

questions.stem: What is the last digit of 2²⁰²⁷ + 3²⁰²⁷ + 7²⁰²⁷?
questions.explanation: Last digits of powers repeat every 4 exponents, and 2027 mod 4 = 3. So 2²⁰²⁷ ends like 2³ = 8, 3²⁰²⁷ like 3³ = 27, giving 7, and 7²⁰²⁷ like 7³ = 343, giving 3. The sum of last digits is 8 + 7 + 3 = 18, so the last digit is 8.

pitfalls.text: Reading "Some A are B" as also saying "Some A are not B". In logic "some" means at least one and allows all.
Converting "All A are B" into "All B are A". Only "Some B are A" follows.
Using real-world knowledge to accept or reject a syllogism conclusion. The premises are taken as true, however absurd.
Picking the converse of a conditional. "If P then Q" does not give "If Q then P" or "If not P then not Q".
Answering the direction of the end point when the question asks for the start point with respect to the end point.
Fixing gender from a name in a blood-relation puzzle. Only gendered words such as he, she, son or mother fix it.
Mixing up left and right for people facing the centre of a table or facing south in a row. Decide the facing direction before placing anyone.
Stopping at the first consistent arrangement. A puzzle answer is safe only when every surviving case gives the same fact.

Some = at least one, possibly all
All A–B + All B–C = All A–C; Some A–B + No B–C = Some A not C
Two "Some" premises: no definite link; check for an either-or pair

Converse and inverse are not equivalent to P → Q

revisionCard.heading: Relations, directions, ranks

Track (x, y); distance √(x² + y²); start-from-end is the reverse vector
N → E → S → W is clockwise; right = +90°
Total = rank from top + rank from bottom − 1

lines: Data sufficiency: a sure "no" is sufficient

EJOTY: E 5, J 10, O 15, T 20, Y 25; mirror letters sum to 27

errata.claim: If both premises are affirmative ("All", "Some"), a negative conclusion ("No", "Some not") is universally false.
errata.correction: Affirmative premises can never prove a negative conclusion, so such a conclusion does not follow; it is not false. From "All A are B" and "Some B are C", "Some A are not C" is true in some diagrams and false in others.

errata.claim: In "He is the son of the only son of my mother", the phrase "only son" forces the speaker Suresh to be male, so Suresh is the boy's father.
errata.correction: The phrase does not force the speaker's gender. If the speaker is male, the only son of his mother is himself and he is the boy's father; if the speaker were female, that son is her brother and she is the boy's aunt. The answer "father" rests on reading Suresh as male, the same name-based assumption the pronoun trap warns against.

errata.claim: Seating problem 22: A sits in the north seat of a square table facing the centre and B sits to A's immediate right; the answer is given first as "West" for the direction B faces.
errata.correction: A faces south, so A's right is the west seat. B sits in the west seat and, facing the centre, faces east. "West" is B's seat, not the direction B faces.
